title: NL Injury Update: Freeman, Henriquez, Elder, Ortiz, Woodruff Out – Trade Rumors Ignite MLB Market
body:
The Los Angeles Dodgers, Atlanta Braves and Milwaukee Brewers entered the postseason with a mix of optimism and lingering injury concerns, as updates on key players emerged on the eve of the National League Division Series. Freddie Freeman, the Dodgers’ first‑base stalwart, confirmed he is fully healthy after a brief stint on the injured list, while Atlanta’s left‑handed reliever Dylan Henriquez and Milwaukee’s veteran outfielder Christian Woodruff are both expected to be cleared for action. The latest medical reports, however, also highlighted setbacks for the Dodgers’ shortstop Gavin Elder and the Braves’ starting pitcher Austin Ortiz, casting a shadow over their respective rotations as the clubs prepare for a grueling three‑week playoff run.

Freeman’s return was the most reassuring news for Los Angeles. The 34‑year‑old first baseman missed two weeks after a strained right hamstring, but a recent interview with the Orange County Register confirmed he has completed a full rehab regimen and is back to his pre‑injury form. “I feel 100 percent,” Freeman said, adding that the extra days off have actually helped him fine‑tune his swing. His presence in the middle of the lineup is crucial; he finished the regular season with a .307 average, 23 home runs and a league‑leading OPS above .950. With the Dodgers poised to chase a historic three‑peat, Freeman’s health not only stabilizes the offensive core but also provides a veteran anchor for a clubhouse that has already endured a season of injuries.

Atlanta’s bullpen, meanwhile, received a boost with the clearance of Dylan Henriquez, who was placed on the 10‑day injured list after a right‑elbow strain in late September. Henriquez, a 26‑year‑old left‑hander who posted a 2.87 ERA over 57 innings this year, is expected to rejoin the relievers’ roster ahead of Game 1 of the NLDS. The Braves, however, will have to navigate the loss of Austin Ortiz, a right‑handed starter who suffered a left‑shoulder impingement during the final series of the regular season. Ortiz’s injury required a short stint on the IL, and while imaging suggests a minor tear, the team’s medical staff is cautious, indicating he may miss the first two starts of the series. This development forces Atlanta’s manager to lean more heavily on the depth of his rotation, potentially elevating rookie right‑hander Jace Miller into a spot‑start role.

Milwaukee’s situation is a study in contrasts. The Brewers have cleared Christian Woodruff, the 31‑year‑old outfielder who was sidelined with a Grade‑2 hamstring strain after a hard‑fought series against the Cardinals. Woodruff’s speed and defensive versatility have been missed, but his return is expected to be seamless; he logged 15 innings in a rehab assignment and displayed the same range that helped the Brewers secure a wild‑card berth. Conversely, shortstop Gavin Elder, who suffered a fractured right wrist in the final weekend, remains on the injured list. Elder’s absence leaves a hole in the middle infield, prompting manager Craig Counsell to consider a hybrid solution with utility man Aramis Ramirez shifting between second base and shortstop. The Brewers’ offense, already reliant on power from William Contreras and Ryan Lindsey, will need Elder’s bat to sustain momentum against a deep NL East opponent.

The injury updates underscore a broader theme across the National League: depth and adaptability are now as valuable as star power. For the Dodgers, the combination of Freeman’s health and a rested pitching staff could translate into a dominant offensive showcase, but the lingering uncertainty surrounding Elder may limit their defensive flexibility. Atlanta’s bullpen gains a left‑handed option in Henriquez, yet the potential loss of Ortiz could strain a rotation already taxed by a grueling regular season. Milwaukee’s ability to reintegrate Woodruff while compensating for Elder’s wrist will test the club’s strategic ingenuity.

Looking ahead, the next few days will determine how each franchise’s medical and coaching staffs balance caution with competitiveness. If Freeman continues to thrive and Henriquez provides the left‑handed depth the Braves need, both teams could enter the series with a clear advantage. The Brewers, meanwhile, must find a way to mitigate Elder’s loss without sacrificing offensive output. As the NLDS tip‑off approaches, the health of these key contributors will likely shape not only the opening games but also the trajectory of each team’s postseason aspirations.
